questions.stem: Minutes after an IV antibiotic begins, a client develops stridor, diffuse wheezing, hives, and blood pressure of 78/44 mm Hg. Which intervention has the highest priority?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Give intramuscular epinephrine in the mid-outer thigh promptly while activating emergency support and beginning airway and circulatory measures.","B":"Administer IV diphenhydramine first, then reassess the blood pressure before deciding whether epinephrine is necessary for persistent symptoms.","C":"Start an albuterol nebulizer first because bronchospasm is the most immediate threat, then give epinephrine if wheezing does not resolve fully.","D":"Give IV corticosteroid first to suppress the allergic response, then add epinephrine if hypotension remains after the steroid has begun working."}}
questions.rationale: This presentation is anaphylaxis with airway, bronchospastic, cutaneous, and circulatory involvement. Intramuscular epinephrine in the mid-outer thigh is the first-line, time-critical treatment and should be given promptly while airway, oxygenation, circulation, emergency support, and additional resuscitative measures are addressed. Antihistamines, bronchodilators, and corticosteroids may have adjunctive roles but must not delay epinephrine.
questions.source_name: AAAAI/ACAAI Joint Task Force — Anaphylaxis: A 2023 Practice Parameter Update
questions.source_detail: Primary guideline publication: Ann Allergy Asthma Immunol. 2024;132(2):124-176; DOI 10.1016/j.anai.2023.09.015. Epinephrine remains first-line treatment for anaphylaxis; current AAAAI implementation guidance specifies prompt IM epinephrine in the mid-outer thigh.

questions.stem: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used hollow-bore needle. The source patient’s bloodborne-infection status is not yet known. Which action should the nurse take first?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Squeeze the puncture until it bleeds freely, apply a concentrated antiseptic, and wait for the source patient’s laboratory results before reporting the exposure.","B":"Cover the puncture with an occlusive dressing and finish the current medication round, then report the exposure at the end of the shift if symptoms develop.","C":"Request testing of the source patient first and delay personal evaluation until infection status is confirmed, because prophylaxis is unnecessary after an unknown exposure.","D":"Wash the puncture site promptly with soap and water, report the exposure immediately, and obtain urgent occupational-exposure evaluation for indicated prophylaxis."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA directs workers with needlestick or blood exposure to immediately clean the wound with soap and water, report the incident immediately, and seek immediate medical attention. Post-exposure evaluation should not be delayed while waiting for the source patient’s test results because time-sensitive prophylaxis may be indicated. Squeezing the wound or delaying reporting does not replace prompt first aid and exposure evaluation.
questions.source_detail: 29 CFR 1910.1030(d)(2)(vi): wash exposed skin with soap and water immediately/as soon as feasible; 1910.1030(f)(3): following a reported exposure incident, confidential post-exposure evaluation and follow-up must be made immediately available.

questions.stem: Minutes after an IV antibiotic begins, a client develops generalized hives, wheezing, facial swelling, and hypotension. Which medication should the nurse prepare to give first for the suspected anaphylaxis?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"IV diphenhydramine because antihistamine therapy reverses the airway and circulatory manifestations of anaphylaxis more rapidly than epinephrine.","B":"IV methylprednisolone because corticosteroids provide the fastest treatment for acute hypotension and bronchospasm during anaphylaxis.","C":"Intramuscular epinephrine in the mid-outer thigh while emergency support, airway assessment, and additional resuscitation measures are initiated.","D":"Nebulized albuterol alone because bronchodilation treats the life-threatening component of anaphylaxis even when hypotension is also present."}}
questions.rationale: Current anaphylaxis guidance continues to identify prompt intramuscular epinephrine in the mid-outer thigh as first-line treatment. Antihistamines, corticosteroids, and inhaled bronchodilators may have adjunctive roles but do not replace epinephrine for a systemic reaction with airway/breathing and circulatory compromise.

questions.stem: A client arrives with repeated hematemesis, heart rate 126/min, blood pressure 84/50 mm Hg, cool clammy skin, and dizziness. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's priority assessment?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings indicate hemodynamic compromise from acute blood loss and require immediate escalation rather than routine evaluation as a stable gastrointestinal bleed.","B":"The findings are compatible with a stable upper gastrointestinal bleed because the client remains awake, so routine diagnostic sequencing can proceed without urgent escalation.","C":"The low blood pressure is most consistent with an isolated medication effect because acute gastrointestinal blood loss usually causes bradycardia before circulatory compromise.","D":"The cool skin and dizziness are expected anxiety responses and do not materially change urgency unless laboratory testing first confirms a major fall in hemoglobin."}}
questions.rationale: Tachycardia, marked hypotension, cool clammy skin, and dizziness in a client with ongoing hematemesis indicate hemodynamic compromise from acute blood loss. Current upper-GI-bleeding guidance emphasizes rapid recognition and stabilization of hemodynamically unstable patients before routine diagnostic sequencing. Preserved consciousness does not make this presentation stable.
questions.source_name: American College of Gastroenterology — Clinical Guideline: Upper Gastrointestinal and Ulcer Bleeding
questions.source_detail: Primary guideline publication: Am J Gastroenterol. 2021;116(5):899-917; DOI 10.14309/ajg.0000000000001245. Applies to overt upper GI bleeding; hemodynamically unstable presentations require immediate assessment/resuscitative management rather than routine low-risk sequencing.

questions.stem: A client presents with abrupt severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and a serum lipase level greater than three times the upper limit of normal. The client also has known gallstones. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The presentation supports acute pancreatitis because characteristic epigastric pain plus a lipase level more than three times the upper limit of normal meet accepted diagnostic criteria.","B":"The presentation is more consistent with acute cholecystitis because gallstones explain the pain pattern, whereas marked lipase elevation may occur without clinically important pancreatic inflammation.","C":"The presentation remains indeterminate until CT confirms pancreatic inflammation because pain and elevated pancreatic enzymes cannot establish acute pancreatitis without imaging.","D":"The presentation is most consistent with uncomplicated biliary colic because pain after a fatty meal is typical, while pancreatic enzyme elevation commonly accompanies gallstone pain without pancreatitis."}}
questions.rationale: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when at least two of three accepted features are present: characteristic abdominal pain, pancreatic enzymes greater than three times the upper limit of normal, or characteristic imaging findings. This client already has characteristic pain and marked lipase elevation, so CT confirmation is not required to establish the diagnosis. Gallstones are a common cause of acute pancreatitis and make a biliary etiology plausible.
questions.source_name: American College of Gastroenterology — Guidelines: Management of Acute Pancreatitis
questions.source_detail: Primary guideline publication: Am J Gastroenterol. 2024;119(3):419-437; DOI 10.14309/ajg.0000000000002645. Acute pancreatitis is established by the accepted diagnostic framework when at least two of characteristic pain, pancreatic enzymes >3× ULN, or characteristic imaging are present; routine CT is unnecessary when diagnosis is clinically established.

questions.stem: Several hours after thyroid surgery, a client develops new perioral tingling, carpal spasm when a blood-pressure cuff is inflated, and a prolonged QT interval. The measured serum calcium is low. Which interpretation is most accurate?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"The findings are most consistent with symptomatic hypocalcemia causing neuromuscular irritability, which warrants prompt evaluation for a postsurgical calcium disorder.","B":"The findings indicate hyperkalemia because potassium elevation commonly produces perioral tingling, carpal spasm with cuff inflation, and prolongation of the QT interval.","C":"The findings are expected after thyroid surgery because transient paresthesias and carpal spasm are common even when calcium homeostasis remains normal.","D":"The findings are most consistent with anxiety-related hyperventilation alone because a low measured calcium level does not contribute to neuromuscular excitability."}}
questions.rationale: Perioral paresthesia, carpal spasm consistent with Trousseau sign, and QT prolongation are classic manifestations of symptomatic hypocalcemia and neuromuscular irritability. After thyroid surgery, impaired parathyroid function is an important cause to consider. These findings should not be dismissed as routine postoperative symptoms or anxiety alone.
questions.source_name: American Thyroid Association — Statement on Postoperative Hypoparathyroidism
questions.source_detail: ATA Surgical Affairs Committee statement, Thyroid. 2018;28(7):830-841; DOI 10.1089/thy.2017.0309. Post-thyroidectomy hypoparathyroidism/hypocalcemia may produce paresthesias and symptomatic neuromuscular manifestations; severe hypocalcemia requires inpatient management. Current ATA 2026 patient guidance continues to identify perioral/finger tingling and muscle twitching/cramping as postoperative hypocalcemia manifestations.

questions.stem: Two hours after thyroidectomy, a client reports increasing neck pressure and difficulty swallowing. The nurse notes new anterior neck swelling and a change in voice. Which interpretation should guide the nurse's priority response?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Suspect a postoperative neck hematoma with possible evolving airway compromise and escalate the assessment immediately rather than treating the symptoms as routine edema.","B":"Interpret the findings as expected postoperative tissue swelling and continue routine observation unless the oxygen saturation falls below the prescribed target.","C":"Attribute the symptoms primarily to transient recurrent-laryngeal-nerve irritation because a hematoma generally causes obvious external bleeding before pressure symptoms.","D":"Treat the swallowing difficulty as postoperative nausea and delay focused airway assessment until analgesia and antiemetic therapy have had time to take effect."}}
questions.rationale: Neck swelling, dysphagia, voice change, and respiratory findings after thyroidectomy can indicate hemorrhage or swelling that threatens the airway. Early focused airway assessment and escalation are required.

questions.source_detail: ATA postoperative thyroid surgery guidance: rapid neck swelling/tightness affecting breathing or swallowing is an emergency requiring immediate medical attention; voice/breathing/swallowing changes after thyroid surgery require prompt assessment.

questions.stem: During a conversation, a distressed client becomes tearful and silent after describing a recent loss. Which nursing response best demonstrates active, therapeutic listening?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Fill the silence by giving advice about coping strategies so the client does not become more uncomfortable or feel pressured to continue talking.","B":"Remain present, allow the silence, and then use an open-ended or reflective statement that invites the client to continue at their own pace.","C":"Ask a series of specific yes-or-no questions to keep the discussion efficient and prevent the client from becoming overwhelmed by emotion.","D":"Change to a neutral topic until the client stops crying because discussing the loss while visibly distressed can reinforce emotional dependence."}}
questions.rationale: Therapeutic listening includes remaining present, tolerating silence, reflecting what was heard, and using open-ended prompts rather than rushing into advice, interrogation, or topic change.
questions.source_name: SAMHSA — How to Talk to Someone About Help
questions.source_detail: Current SAMHSA guidance recommends listening without judgment, reflecting what is heard, and using open-ended questions rather than forcing or rushing the conversation.
